title: Alkenes: the π bond is the nucleophile
review: Step 10 compares three ways to hydrate 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene: H2SO4/H2O gives 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol (methyl shift), oxymercuration gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, hydroboration gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol. Please confirm the wording of step 5 (mercurinium described as bridged like bromonium).

steps.text: An alkene's **π bond** is a pair of electrons sitting above and below the C=C, so the alkene is the **nucleophile**. It attacks an electrophile (H⁺, Br2, Hg(OAc)⁺, BH3). With HX, H adds to the carbon that leaves the **more stable carbocation** (3° > 2° > 1°). That's **Markovnikov's rule**.
Two steps: the π bond grabs H⁺ to make the 3° cation, then bromide adds to it.

A carbocation can **rearrange** before the nucleophile arrives. If a neighbouring carbon carries an H or a CH3 that could move over and leave a more stable cation (2° → 3°), it shifts with its bonding pair: a **1,2-hydride** or **1,2-methyl shift**. Watch for a 2° cation next to a branch.
Protonate, check the neighbour, then add Cl⁻.

Br2 and Hg(OAc)2 don't make a free carbocation. The electrophile **bridges** both carbons (a bromonium or mercurinium ion). So nothing rearranges, and the nucleophile must attack from the **opposite face**: **anti** addition. It opens the bridge at the more substituted carbon.
The π bond's arrow is drawn. Add the rest: Br⁻ leaves, and the near Br bridges back to the other carbon.
Cyclohexene + Br2 gives only **trans**-1,2-dibromocyclohexane. Why no cis?

options.text: The bromonium ion blocks one face, so Br⁻ has to attack from the other face (anti addition).
options.explains: Right. Backside opening of the bridged ion puts the two Br atoms on opposite faces.

options.text: The trans isomer is more stable, so the cis isomer converts into it.
options.explains: The product doesn't equilibrate; stereochemistry is fixed by the mechanism. Anti attack on the bromonium ion makes trans directly.

options.text: A planar carbocation forms, and Br⁻ attacks it from the less hindered side.
options.explains: A free carbocation could be attacked from either face and give both isomers. The bridged bromonium ion is why only trans forms.

options.text: Both Br atoms add at the same time from the same molecule of Br2.
options.explains: That would be syn addition and would give cis. The two Br atoms arrive in separate steps from opposite faces.

steps.text: **Hydroboration** is different again: BH3 adds in **one concerted step**. Boron goes to the **less substituted** carbon and H to the other, on the **same face** (syn). No cation, no rearrangement. H2O2/NaOH then swaps B for OH with retention: an **anti-Markovnikov**, syn alcohol.
Think about which face B and H arrive on.

options.explains: Right. Markovnikov (OH on the inner carbon) through a bridged mercurinium ion, so the tert-butyl group's methyls don't shift.
Markovnikov, but through a free 2° carbocation that does a methyl shift: you get 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov: the OH goes on the CH2 end (3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol).
Peroxides give the anti-Markovnikov 1° bromide, and on that route the OH would end up on the end carbon, not the inner one.
